question: Are we eligible for PMMVY for our first baby?
answer:

It supports pregnant and lactating mothers under the National Food Security Act, 2013 (INDIA-PMMVY, p. 2). The passages don't list every eligibility rule, such as income, employment or age limits. So I can't say for certain that you qualify. Please check with your Anganwadi or ASHA worker, or call the helpline 14408 (INDIA-PMMVY, p. 7).

To apply, you'd need the Mother and Child Protection (MCP) Card and eligibility proof such as a BPL card (INDIA-PMMVY, p. 5). Registration is through the PMMVY portal, the UMANG app, or an Anganwadi/ASHA worker. Aadhaar authentication and a DBT-enabled bank account are checked upfront (INDIA-PMMVY, p. 7). It would help to get your Aadhaar linked to the bank account now.

Separately, Janani Suraksha Yojana gives cash help for delivering in a government facility (INDIA-JSY, p. 4). Your local health worker can confirm the current amounts for your state.

question: What are JSY and JSSK and could we use them for delivery?
answer:
Both are government schemes for delivery, and you may well be able to use them. Please confirm details with your local ASHA/ANM, since the JSY passage is Odisha's guideline and states can differ.

JSY (Janani Suraksha Yojana) is a safe-motherhood scheme that gives cash assistance and supports delivery and post-delivery care, to promote institutional delivery (INDIA-JSY, p. 3). All pregnant women delivering in government health centres are eligible. In accredited private institutions, only families with a BPL card or SC/ST certificate qualify (INDIA-JSY, p. 4). In Odisha, the cash is Rs 1400 for the mother in rural areas and Rs 1000 in urban areas (INDIA-JSY, p. 4). A JSY card is issued with the MCH card at registration or first ANC, and you carry it to the delivery (INDIA-JSY, p. 21).

JSSK (Janani Shishu Suraksha Karyakaram) aims to remove out-of-pocket costs. Every pregnant woman delivering in a public facility is entitled to free delivery, including caesarean, with free transport, diet, diagnostics, medicines and blood if needed (INDIA-JSSK, p. 2). Free diet is 3 days after vaginal delivery and 7 days after caesarean (INDIA-JSSK, p. v).

At 22 weeks, a good next step is to ask your ASHA or ANM about registration.

question: We follow a strict Jain diet. What can the breastfeeding parent eat while meeting nutrition needs?
answer:
Congratulations on your little one. Breastfeeding needs extra food: about 600 extra calories and 13.6 g extra protein daily in the first six months, and slightly less (520 calories, 10.6 g protein) in the next six (ICMR-NIN-DG, p. 32). A Jain diet can meet much of this with familiar foods:

- Eat extra cereals, pulses and vegetables, 5-6 times a day if big meals are hard (MOHFW-IYCF, p. 177).
- Cereal plus pulse in a 3:1 mix gives good protein (ICMR-NIN-DG, p. 32). Paushtik khichari with rice, dal and spinach, plus a little pure ghee, is a good example (MOHFW-IYCF, p. 177).
- Eat green leafy vegetables daily for iron (MOHFW-IYCF, p. 177). Beans, dry fruits and pulses also give iron; sprouted or fermented grains and vitamin C fruits like guava or oranges help absorption (ICMR-NIN-DG, p. 32).
- Milk is the best calcium source but poor in iron (ICMR-NIN-DG, p. 32).
- Have 1-2 fruits daily (MOHFW-IYCF, p. 177), use iodized salt, and get some sunlight for vitamin D (ICMR-NIN-DG, p. 32).

Please choose non-root vegetables such as bottle gourd and spinach. Your doctor will advise on iron and folic acid tablets, which are recommended during lactation (ICMR-NIN-DG, p. 32).

The certificate is a legal document needed later, for example for school admission (MOHFW-ANC, p. 62).

question: Is it okay to drink coffee while pregnant?
answer: Good news: you don't have to give up coffee. WHO recommends that women who have a high daily caffeine intake (more than 300 mg a day) cut down, because high intake is probably linked to a higher risk of pregnancy loss and low birth weight (WHO-ANC, p. 38). In the studies, low intake (under 150 mg a day) was not linked to more pregnancy loss (WHO-ANC, p. 39). Caffeine counts from all sources, including tea, cola, chocolate and energy drinks. A cup of instant coffee has about 60 mg, but some brewed coffees have over 150 mg per serving. Black or green tea usually has under 50 mg per 250 mL (WHO-ANC, p. 38). So the type and size of your cup matter. Many people find it helpful to keep a rough count of their daily cups. Please check with your doctor about what suits your health and pregnancy, and mention it at your next antenatal visit, especially if you usually drink a lot of coffee or other caffeinated drinks.

question: My wife has morning sickness. How can I help without forcing her to eat?
answer: It's lovely that you want to help. Morning sickness in the first trimester may be physiological, and the guidance is gentle rather than forceful (MOHFW-ANC, p. 37). Things you can do: offer small, frequent meals instead of big ones; keep greasy and spicy food out of the house; and encourage plenty of fluids. If mornings are the worst, keep dry foods like roti, paratha, biscuits or toast by the bed for her to eat after waking (MOHFW-ANC, p. 37). Bring home foods she fancies from the recommended list, such as curd, fruits, pulses and green vegetables (MOHFW-ANC, p. 30), keeping her tastes and local produce in mind (MOHFW-ANC, p. 31). Take on household chores so she can rest (MOHFW-ANC, p. 31). Please don't give her any medicine unless a qualified doctor prescribes it (MOHFW-ANC, p. 31). If her vomiting becomes excessive, or she seems dehydrated (dry tongue, passing very little urine), take her to the doctor promptly (MOHFW-ANC, p. 37).

The guidelines also advise that family members who decide what food is brought home be included in diet counselling (MOHFW-ANC, p. 30), so you could share this with them or bring them to a check-up. For how much ghee is right for you, please ask your doctor.

question: Can I fast for Navratri while pregnant?
answer: Navratri is meaningful, and your wish to honour it is understandable. The passages I have don't speak directly about fasting in pregnancy, so I can't say whether it is safe for you. I don't have a trusted source for that. Please ask your doctor, ideally at your 26-week contact (WHO-ANC, p. 105). What the sources do say: a pregnant woman needs about 300 extra kcal a day, should eat more than usual, and can eat 5-6 times a day (MOHFW-ANC, p. 30; MOHFW-IYCF, p. 177). Diet should include protein, iron and vitamin C-rich foods, and your family can be involved to help you eat enough (MOHFW-ANC, p. 30-31). Food customs that limit nutritionally important foods should be discussed with your care provider (MOHFW-ANC, p. 31). Please also keep taking iron and folic acid as advised (WHO-ANC, p. 108), and take no medicine unless a qualified practitioner prescribes it (MOHFW-ANC, p. 31). If you feel dizzy, weak or unwell, see a doctor promptly. Ask your doctor about a gentler way to observe the festival.

question: What are affordable iron-rich vegetarian foods for a pregnant woman in a small Indian town?
answer: At 17 weeks, simple everyday foods can help. Green leafy vegetables like spinach (palak), fenugreek (methi), amaranth, drumstick leaves, mint and coriander are iron sources, and the guidelines suggest about 150g of them daily (ICMR-NIN-DG, p. 33). Try methi or palak roti, or add greens to khichari with dal (ICMR-NIN-DG, p. 34; MOHFW-IYCF, p. 177). Pulses, legumes, beans, dry fruits and nuts also contain iron, and vegetarians can use legumes and pulses in place of meat, fish and eggs (ICMR-NIN-DG, p. 36; MOHFW-IYCF, p. 177). Iron from plant foods is absorbed less well, so add vitamin C fruits such as guava, lemon or orange with meals (ICMR-NIN-DG, p. 36). Avoid tea or coffee with meals or soon after, as it blocks iron (ICMR-NIN-DG, p. 36). Eating 5-6 small meals a day can help if you feel full quickly (MOHFW-IYCF, p. 177). Anganwadi centres may offer supplementary nutrition (ICMR-NIN-DG, p. 34). I don't have prices from my sources, so I can't say which of these is cheapest in your town. Your doctor will advise on iron and folic acid tablets and check your haemoglobin.

question: My mother says drinking saffron milk makes the baby fair. Is that true?
answer: It's lovely that your mother wants the best for you and the baby. None of the passages I have mention saffron, or say that any food or drink changes a baby's skin colour, so I don't have a trusted source for that. Please ask your doctor. What the sources do say is that your diet should suit your food habits and what is available locally, with iron-rich foods and vitamin C foods like amla, guava, lemon or oranges to help iron absorption, and enough fibre to avoid constipation (MOHFW-ANC, p. 31). If a family custom involves leaving out nutritionally important foods, the guidance is to gently advise against that taboo (MOHFW-ANC, p. 31). Please don't take any medication unless a qualified health practitioner prescribes it (MOHFW-ANC, p. 31). If you'd like to keep the saffron milk as a family tradition, check with your doctor that it suits you. You are doing well at 27 weeks, and your doctor can answer any worries about your baby's growth.

question: What should I ask during my first ultrasound appointment?
answer: At 10 weeks, a first scan is a lovely milestone. The passages don't give a ready-made question list for an ultrasound visit, but they do show what an early scan is meant to look at, so you can ask about these things. WHO says the scan's purpose is to check: where the pregnancy is located (for example inside the uterus), the baby's heartbeat (cardiac activity), the baby's size, gestational age (how many weeks along you are, which helps with your due date), and whether it is one baby or more (WHO-ANC-ULTRASOUND, p. 16). You could ask, 'Is the heartbeat seen? Does the size match my weeks? Is it one baby?' Detailed checks of the baby's body parts and the placenta are more informative after 18 weeks, so you may be offered a later scan for that (WHO-ANC-ULTRASOUND, p. 16). Also ask whether the person scanning is trained in obstetric ultrasound (WHO-ANC-ULTRASOUND, p. 16). It helps to mention any past pregnancy problems or family history of twins or birth defects (MOHFW-ANC, p. 15; p. 16). I can't see any scan report you may have, so please share your doctor's explanation or ask them directly if anything worries you.

question: Do I need Td vaccination during pregnancy in India?
answer: Yes, Td is part of routine antenatal care in India. India's immunization schedule lists Td-1, Td-2 or a Td booster for pregnant women (INDIA-UIP, p. 4). Which one you need depends on your earlier tetanus vaccines. Td-1 is given as early as possible in pregnancy, and Td-2 follows 4 weeks later. A booster is given instead if you had 2 Td doses within the last 3 years. Td-2 or the booster is preferably given before 36 weeks (INDIA-UIP, p. 5). At 20 weeks you are well within that window. WHO also recommends tetanus vaccination for all pregnant women, depending on past vaccination, to protect the baby from neonatal tetanus. Evidence shows at least two doses greatly reduce neonatal tetanus deaths, with no sign of harm to mothers or babies (WHO-ANC, pp. 70-71). A sore arm can happen (WHO-ANC, p. 71). Please keep your vaccination records handy and ask your doctor or ANC clinic which dose you need. I can't see your records, so they can check your history and decide. If you haven't had a dose yet, ask at your next visit.

question: My glucose test was flagged high. Can I fix gestational diabetes by avoiding rice completely?
answer: I'm sorry the result worried you; a flagged test is not a diagnosis, and many women are in the same place at this stage. The usual window for GDM testing is 24 to 28 weeks (WHO-ANC, p. 48), so your timing is typical. Your doctor needs to look at your actual numbers to confirm what this means. I don't have a trusted source on whether cutting out rice completely helps, so please don't drop a whole food on your own. Skipping meals or restricting too much without guidance may not be safe, and your doctor or a dietitian should decide what suits you and your baby. What the source does say: GDM treatment usually starts with lifestyle changes like nutritional counselling and exercise, and treatment is effective in reducing poor outcomes (WHO-ANC, p. 48). Diet and exercise support may also lower GDM risk (WHO-ANC, p. 16). Please book a follow-up soon, and ask: Is this GDM? What should I eat, and how much rice or other foods are fine? How often should my sugar be checked? Whether any medicine is needed is your doctor's decision.

question: Can I take an overnight bus at 36 weeks to go to my parents house for delivery?
answer:
I'm glad you're planning ahead. I don't have a trusted source on whether an overnight bus at 36 weeks is safe, so please ask your doctor before you book. What my sources do say may help you plan. Pre-term labour means labour starting before 37 weeks, and at 36 weeks you are still within that window (MOHFW-ANC, p. 81). Delay in reaching a facility is a major cause of maternal deaths, so it helps to have transport ready (MOHFW-ANC, p. 28). Before you travel, ask your doctor, and also:
- Find out which 24-hour PHC or FRU is near your parents' home and how to reach it (MOHFW-ANC, p. 29).
- Save the ambulance number (108; 102 for free transport to a government hospital) (MOHFW-ANC, p. 28).
- Carry your MCP card and all antenatal records, scans and test reports (MOHFW-ANC, p. 28).
- Decide who will travel with you (MOHFW-ANC, p. 29).
Signs of labour are a bloody sticky discharge or painful contractions that grow stronger and closer together; go to a facility without waiting if they begin (MOHFW-ANC, p. 28).

question: I feel anxious about labour and everyone says I should just be happy.
answer: Feeling anxious about labour is very understandable, and your feelings matter, even when others say you should just be happy. Being both excited and nervous is normal. The passages don't cover anxiety itself, so please share this worry with your doctor or midwife, especially if it's affecting your sleep, eating or daily life. Some things in the guidelines may be reassuring. Birth attendants are meant to give emotional support as well as physical care (MOHFW-ANC, p. 39). You can choose the position you find comfortable in labour (MOHFW-ANC, p. 39), and you should be told what is being done and asked for consent before a vaginal examination (MOHFW-ANC, p. 41). You can eat light food and drink as you wish during labour (MOHFW-ANC, p. 41). A first labour usually takes about 12 hours in the first stage (MOHFW-ANC, p. 43), and you won't be left alone (MOHFW-ANC, p. 47). Try writing down your questions and asking your care team to walk you through what to expect. If the anxiety feels overwhelming, please see your doctor soon.

question: My neighbour gave me herbal kadha for contractions. Should I take it?
answer: It's kind of your neighbour to share this. Since you are at 32 weeks, I can't say whether you should take the kadha, and I can't name or judge any herbal remedy. None of my sources say what is in it or whether it is safe in pregnancy. Please show it to your doctor or pharmacist before trying it, because the right choice depends on your health and your pregnancy. You could ask them: what is in it, and is it safe for me and my baby right now? The WHO notes that many women turn to herbal remedies and traditional healers, and that care works best when your beliefs and traditions are respected (WHO-ANC, p. 78). Your doctor can do that. At 32 weeks, tightening may be false labour pain. This tends to stay irregular, stay in the abdomen and groin, and ease with walking or sleep. True labour pain becomes regular and stronger, starts in the lower back, and may come with a blood-stained 'show' (MOHFW-ANC, p. 43). If your pains are regular, getting stronger, or you see a show or any bleeding, please contact your doctor or go to a hospital right away, as this is early.

question: I had a C-section. How should I plan help at home in the first two weeks?
answer: Congratulations, and well done on recovering from major surgery. The passages don't give C-section-specific advice on household help, lifting or wound care, so please ask your surgeon about those. What they do support is planning around the first two weeks. WHO calls the first two weeks a key time to spot problems and support the move to the home (WHO-POSTNATAL, p. 152). Practical steps: 1) Decide who looks after the home, cooking and other children, as Nestling's checklist suggests for birth planning (MOHFW-ANC, p. 29). 2) Before discharge, ask the team to go over how you will manage at home and what your home setup is like (WHO-POSTNATAL, p. xiv). 3) Ask for a home visit in the first week by a health worker, or an outpatient visit if home visits aren't possible (WHO-POSTNATAL, p. xiv). 4) Plan check-ups at 48-72 hours and at 7-14 days (WHO-POSTNATAL, p. 152). 5) Keep ambulance numbers handy: 108, or 102 for free transport to a government hospital (MOHFW-ANC, p. 28). Family helpers can also support breastfeeding, which you should get support with at each contact (WHO-POSTNATAL, p. xiv).

question: My mother-in-law suggests giving honey to my newborn before breastfeeding.
answer: It's lovely that your mother-in-law wants to welcome and care for your baby. On honey, though, the sources I have don't mention it by name, so I can't speak to it specifically. What they do say is clear: breastfed newborns should get nothing except breast milk unless a doctor advises it (WHO-POSTNATAL, p. 149). Breastfeeding should start within the first hour, and only breast milk, not even water, for the first six months (WHO-POSTNATAL, p. 148; MOHFW-ANC, p. 32). Giving other foods or drinks before the first feed is called a pre-lacteal feed. In India it is a common practice, but these feeds may not be hygienic and can cause infections and diarrhoea (MOHFW-ANC, p. 32). Your first milk, colostrum, is not harmful; it is rich in protective antibodies (MOHFW-ANC, p. 32). You could gently tell her that the doctors advise your baby's first food to be your milk, and that you'd love her help with comfort, rest and support. If you're unsure, or the baby has already been given something and seems unwell, please speak to your paediatrician or nurse.

question: I feel I have too little milk on day three. Should I switch to formula?
answer: It's very common to worry about this on day three, and you're not alone. In the first few days your breasts make colostrum in small amounts (30-90 ml), which is enough for a normal newborn (MOHFW-IYCF, p. 80). Almost all mothers can make enough milk if the baby suckles well and often, and the more the baby suckles, the more milk you make (MOHFW-IYCF, p. 81). Reliable signs of enough milk are weight gain and about six wet nappies a day once feeding is established; the usual causes of low intake are feeding too rarely, a poor latch, or short feeds (MOHFW-IYCF, pp. 81, 123). Feeding at least 8 times a day, and offering bottles or other fluids less, helps keep your supply up (MOHFW-IYCF, p. 123). WHO recommends exclusive breastfeeding from birth to 6 months, with support at each postnatal contact (WHO-POSTNATAL, p. xiv). Please don't decide on formula alone: ask your doctor, nurse or a skilled breastfeeding counsellor to watch a feed and check your baby's weight. Please see them soon if you're worried or your baby seems unwell.

question: My family wants me to eat only rice and rasam after delivery. Is that enough?
answer: Congratulations, and thank you for asking. Rice and rasam alone is not enough while you breastfeed. Your body needs extra food: about 600 extra calories and 13.6 g more protein daily in the first six months (ICMR-NIN-DG, p. 32). Aim for a mixed diet, eating 5-6 times a day, with cereals plus pulses plus vegetables (MOHFW-IYCF, p. 177). Rice with dal and green leafy vegetables, like a paushtik khichari with a little ghee, covers many needs in one bowl (MOHFW-IYCF, p. 177). Eat green leafy vegetables daily for iron, and 1-2 fruits a day (MOHFW-IYCF, p. 177). Vitamin C foods like guava or oranges with meals help your body use iron (ICMR-NIN-DG, p. 32). If you eat eggs, fish or meat, they are good foods; vegetarians can use pulses, beans and legumes instead (MOHFW-IYCF, p. 177). Rasam can stay as part of your meals, just not the whole meal. Your doctor will advise on iron and folic acid tablets, which are recommended during breastfeeding (ICMR-NIN-DG, p. 32). You could share this with your family kindly, and ask your doctor or ASHA worker to explain too.

question: Can I give water to my two-month-old in Bengaluru summer?
answer: It's lovely that you're thinking about your baby's comfort in the heat. For a two-month-old who is breastfed, no water is needed, even in a hot Bengaluru summer. The guidelines say breast milk has enough water to quench the baby's thirst, even in the peak of summer, for the first six months (MOHFW-ANC, p. 32). Another source states plainly that a breastfeeding baby does not need extra water in hot weather (MOHFW-IYCF, p. 80). So you can simply offer the breast more often, whenever your baby shows hunger or thirst cues (MOHFW-ANC, p. 62). Feeding on demand is encouraged over feeding by the clock (MOHFW-ANC, p. 32). Many families give water out of love, and that's understandable, but the sources advise against it. If your baby seems unusually sleepy, is feeding poorly, or you are worried about dehydration or breastfeeding difficulties, please see your doctor. My passages don't cover what to do if your baby is not breastfed, so please ask your doctor about that.
